title: The law firm with 14 skills
scenario:
You are the operations director of a law firm with 200 staff. After a six-month pilot, lawyers and paralegals have built shared AI skills for contract review, filing and billing notes. Nobody planned who owns them.

The managing partner asks you to "get this under control before we open it to everyone". The exhibit shows the current state.
exhibit:
AI tool at the firm: current state (made-up example data)

Workspace roles
  Admin role holders: 9  (3 IT staff + 6 lawyers from the pilot group)
  Reason given: "pilot lawyers need to try new features"

Shared skills in use: 14
  With a named owner:              9
  With a review date:              4
  That run scripts:                3
  That fetch outside web pages:    2
  Reviewed by someone other than
  the author:                      3

Skill "clause-fetcher" (built by an associate)
  Runs a script that downloads sample clauses from a public website
  Owner: none     Reviewer: the same associate     Review date: none

Access note
  A new paralegal got an AI seat last week. She asks: "Can the assistant now
  open any client file in the document system?"

questions.prompt: Nine people hold the Admin role. What should you do?

options.text: Keep all nine, because pilot lawyers should always be allowed to try new features.
options.explanation: Trying features is a feature permission. OpenAI's guide says to keep built-in administration roles for people who administer the workspace.

options.text: Remove the six lawyers from Admin and give them a custom role for the features.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI separates administrative authority (built-in roles) from feature access (custom roles), and says to limit admin roles to those who administer.

options.text: Remove all nine, so that nobody has Admin rights and the settings stay fixed.
options.explanation: Someone has to administer the workspace. The three IT staff still need the role.

options.text: Give the Admin role to every pilot lawyer so that their rights are all the same.
options.explanation: This adds more admins, not fewer. It goes against the advice to keep the role limited.

questions.prompt: The clause-fetcher skill runs a script and downloads pages from a public website. Its author is also its only reviewer. What is the right next step?

options.text: Keep it live, because the associate knows the skill best and is the right one to approve it.
options.explanation: Anthropic says skill authors should not be their own reviewers. Knowing a skill well is not the same as an independent check.

options.text: Delete every skill that runs a script, because scripts are not allowed at all.
options.explanation: Anthropic rates scripts as high concern, not as banned. They need a review. Three skills run scripts.

options.text: Pause it until a different reviewer checks the script and web address, and sets an owner.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic rates code execution and outside web calls as high concern and asks for a review by someone other than the author. OpenAI also asks for an accountable owner and a review date.

options.text: Leave it live and ask the associate to review it again next month, with a note.
options.explanation: A second look by the same person is not independent, and the skill keeps running in the meantime.

questions.prompt: According to the exhibit, how many shared skills have no named owner, and what should the firm keep for each skill?

options.text: 5 have no owner. Keep a registry: purpose, owner, version, dependencies, evaluation status.
options.explanation: Right. 14 minus 9 is 5. Anthropic's enterprise page lists these registry fields, and OpenAI asks for an owner and a review date.

options.text: 9 have no owner. Keep only the name of the skill and the date it was created.
options.explanation: 9 skills have an owner. The registry also needs more than a name and a date.

options.text: 10 have no owner. Keep a registry with purpose, owner, version, dependencies and results.
options.explanation: 10 skills have no review date (14 minus 4), but only 5 have no owner.

options.text: 5 have no owner. Keep the skills in each lawyer's private folder, so each person is the owner.
options.explanation: Private copies have no shared owner and no review. The point is one registry with named owners.

questions.prompt: The paralegal asks if her new AI seat lets the assistant open any client file. What is the right answer?

options.text: Yes. A seat in the AI tool gives her access to every system that the firm owns.
options.explanation: OpenAI's page says workspace access does not grant permissions in a connected service.

options.text: Yes, but only if she is also given the Admin role in the AI workspace.
options.explanation: An admin role is about workspace administration. It does not change what the document system allows.

options.text: No, the AI tool never connects to other systems, so the question does not arise.
options.explanation: Tools can connect to other systems through plugins and connectors. The question does arise.

options.text: No. The document system decides what her account may read; check its rules.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI says a request must pass every boundary that applies, and a connected service decides what the signed-in account can read.
